notes: The questions join the temple’s destruction, Jesus’ coming, and the end of the age. The translation does not assign them a single timetable.
“Abomination of desolation” echoes Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11. The reader-directed aside is retained within the passage.
The Greek bird name can denote eagles or vultures. The corpse setting supports “vultures”; the proverb’s precise application is left open.
“The sign of the Son of Man” can be understood in several ways; the text does not identify a separate object. “Earth” can also mean “land.”
The Greek can mean “it is near” or “he is near.”
The text says “this generation.” Its relation to the events described remains debated.
The pinned Greek includes “nor the Son”; some manuscripts omit these words.
The sayings do not explicitly identify whether being taken or being left is the favorable outcome.
The Greek literally describes cutting in two. The violent judgment image is retained.
vocabulary: Greek parousia: arrival or presence; here Jesus’ coming.
Greek oikoumenē: the inhabited world, sometimes viewed in terms of the known world or empire.
A scriptural expression for a desecrating horror associated with devastation.
Greek eklektoi: those selected or chosen; also rendered “elect.”
Jesus’ recurring self-designation; the cloud imagery echoes Daniel 7:13.
Greek doulos can mean an enslaved person. This household role should not be assumed to be modern paid employment.

notes: All ten bridesmaids fall asleep. The story distinguishes their readiness when the bridegroom arrives.
“At once” stands at the verse boundary in the pinned Greek. Here it describes the first servant going to work; it can also be connected with the master’s departure.
The description of the master as harsh begins in the servant’s speech. Verse 26 repeats it as a question.
“These brothers and sisters of mine” may refer specifically to Jesus’ disciples or more broadly to vulnerable people. The phrase is retained without substituting either interpretation.
The same Greek adjective, aiōnios, modifies both punishment and life.
vocabulary: Greek parthenoi: virgins or unmarried young women; here participants awaiting the bridegroom.
Greek lampades may denote lamps or torches; the story requires a supply of oil.
A large weight used as a monetary unit, not an innate skill. Its value depended on the metal and local standard.
Greek aiōnios: eternal, or pertaining to an age; the parallel in this verse is preserved.

notes: The pinned Greek includes “disciples” after “twelve.”
Judas says “Rabbi”; the other disciples say “Lord” in verse 22. “You have said it” retains Jesus’ indirect response.
The pinned Greek reads “the covenant,” without “new,” and includes “for the forgiveness of sins.”
Matthew’s prediction has one rooster-crowing marker. It is not changed to Mark’s twice-crowing form.
Jesus addresses Peter, but “you” in the question is plural, including the others with him.
The opening can also be punctuated as a statement or command: “Sleep on now and rest.” Greek manuscripts do not supply the modern punctuation that settles this choice.
Jesus’ words to Judas are elliptical. “Do what you came for” is one reading; they may also be understood as asking why he has come.
“Power” is a reverent designation for God. The right-hand and cloud images recall Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13.
The text does not specify the target of Peter’s curses.
vocabulary: An ancient designation for a person with a serious skin condition; it need not identify modern Hansen’s disease.
Greek paradidōmi links betrayal, arrest, and delivery into another’s custody throughout the account.
A binding relationship or commitment; the blood language recalls Exodus 24:8.
Here an image for the suffering Jesus faces.
Greek peirasmos can also mean testing or trial.
A large Roman military unit, here applied to angels; the text gives no exact total of angels.
Greek naos refers to the temple building or sanctuary; hieron can refer more broadly to the temple precinct.

notes: The Greek describes remorse or a change of mind. It uses a different verb from Matthew’s usual verb for repentance.
Matthew attributes the quotation to Jeremiah. Its wording closely recalls Zechariah 11:12–13, alongside imagery associated with Jeremiah; the attribution is preserved.
The pinned Greek includes “Jesus” in Barabbas’s name. Many manuscripts omit it.
The blood declaration is spoken by the crowd in this scene. It does not make Jewish people across later generations its speakers. Pilate’s subsequent order to flog and crucify Jesus remains explicit.
The longer fulfillment quotation found in some manuscripts is absent from the pinned Greek here.
Greek “sixth hour” and “ninth hour” are rendered approximately as noon and three in the afternoon. “Land” can also mean “earth.”
Jesus’ cry quotes Psalm 22:1. Matthew preserves the words and supplies their meaning.
Some manuscripts add a sentence about piercing Jesus’ side. The pinned Greek does not include it here.
The account places the appearance of the raised holy people after Jesus’ resurrection. It gives no further account of their lives.
“You have a guard” can also be read as the instruction “Take a guard.”
vocabulary: Payment associated with bringing about a person’s death.
A Roman military unit; its actual size could vary.
A bitter substance. Matthew does not use Mark’s word “myrrh.”
Abandoned or left behind; the cry’s force is retained.
A Roman officer commanding a unit conventionally associated with a hundred soldiers.
The day of preparation before the Sabbath.

notes: Matthew says the women came to see the tomb. The purpose is not expanded with details from another Gospel.
“Has been raised” preserves the Greek passive expression.
“To this day” is the narrator’s temporal perspective. The statement does not assert that every Jewish person accepted the story.
The wording can refer to some disciples or describe the group’s hesitation. Distazō can be rendered “doubt” or “hesitate”; worship and uncertainty stand together in the scene.
“Make disciples” is the central command. The Greek uses the singular “name” while naming Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
“I am with you” recalls the Emmanuel theme in 1:23. “End of the age” is the expression also used in 24:3.
vocabulary: Greek proskyneō can describe bowing down, homage, or worship; here the women grasp Jesus’ feet.
Greek exousia: authority or the right to act.
To form people as learners and followers.
A washing or immersion rite; here into the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
To observe or carry out, not merely to remember information.
